title: Grid prefix channels as repeating rune keys
question: Do suffix streams split by the grid's leading digit recover a known 12-rune opening at an LP2 page start?
reader_question: Have the five grid-prefix groups been tried as separate keys?
summary: Five suffix channels, three declared value mappings, both Vigenère signs and every real key phase gave no exact known opening at the start of any of 55 nonempty LP2 pages.
finding: The channels have 60, 58, 65, 56 and 17 suffixes. Across 58,190 named page configurations and 523,710 fixed 12-rune opening comparisons, none matched. The longest partial opening prefix was three runes. The 17 group-4 hex nibbles were used as 17 values, not padded to bytes; their direct values duplicate the group-4 base-60-digit key.
limitations: Only page-start, uninterrupted repeating-key GP29 Vigenère with two signs was tested. The nine openings are fixed known readings, not a language score. Source idea 12.12 does not give a direction table, origin or route readout, so no traversal was simulated. This does not exclude a later offset, interruption, transposition or another source-defined key derivation.
next_steps: A route version needs a complete five-state direction table, starting cell and readout. A later-position key test should preregister its offsets and validation target.

family.title: Leading-digit channels of the LP2 grid
family.question: Does splitting grid tokens by their leading digit supply a reproducible key or route?

variant.label: Five manuscript-order suffix streams as repeating keys at page starts

scope.representation: Source grid: all 256 two-character tokens from LP2-49–51 in printed sequence. Targets: first 12 rune indices on all 55 nonempty LP2-00–55 pages; nine fixed 12-rune known-reading openings. Source paths and hashes are pinned in plan.json.
scope.procedure: Partition tokens by leading digit 0–4, retaining suffix order. Map suffixes to base-60 digit values modulo 29 or ASCII byte values modulo 29; for group 4 also parse 17 individual hexadecimal nibbles. Use each as a repeating GP29 key under both signs at every phase. Compare first 12 output indices exactly with each fixed opening.
scope.parameters: Channel lengths 60/58/65/56/17; 1,058 named mapping/phase/sign settings including 34 group-4 duplicate settings; 55 target pages; nine openings; 58,190 named page cases and 523,710 exact comparisons.
scope.exclusions: Unspecified prefix-as-direction table and route, bytes formed from an odd nibble count, later ciphertext offsets, key skips, word resets, cross-page state, other alphabets and language scoring.

review.reviewer: Independent complete channel and opening recount in check.py; planted odd-length wrapped-phase controls

reproduction.environment: Python 3 standard library; frozen grid, page files, alphabet and opening traces are pinned by SHA-256 in plan.json.

visuals.caption: The five manuscript-order suffix channels become rune-key candidates. The odd-length group-4 hex stream was never padded to bytes.

article:
## Result

**No suffix channel recovered any of nine fixed 12-rune openings at the start of an unsolved LP2 page.** The test covered every real key phase, both Vigenère signs, and all **55 nonempty pages LP2-00–55**: 58,190 named page configurations and 523,710 exact opening comparisons. The longest partial prefix was **three runes**. This checks one concrete way to use the channels as repeating keys; it does not exclude a later starting position or a different grid readout.

![The 256 grid tokens divide into five prefix channels; suffixes are mapped to rune keys and compared with fixed openings.](experiments/records/grid-prefix-split-openings/channels.svg)

## From grid cells to candidate keys

Each of the 256 two-character grid tokens has a leading digit `0`–`4`. Keeping the suffixes in printed sequence within each leading-digit class produces streams of **60, 58, 65, 56 and 17 symbols**. For each stream, we mapped each suffix to its base-60 digit value modulo 29 or to its ASCII byte value modulo 29. The `4` channel also has a direct hexadecimal-nibble reading, because all 17 suffixes are hex digits. Its exact string is `97DEF756B98A80EB9`.

Those **17 nibbles are not a whole number of bytes**. The test treats them as 17 numbers from 0 to 15, without padding or packing. That happens to give the same GP29 key values as their base-60 digit interpretation; the two named routes are reported, but the identical key was computed only once. There are 1,058 named mapping/phase/sign settings, of which 34 are this duplicate representation; each setting was checked against 55 page starts and nine openings.

For a key `K` and page ciphertext `C`, the test calculated `P[j] = C[j] ± K[(j + phase) mod length(K)] (mod 29)` for the first 12 runes. It used both signs and every phase from zero to the full key length minus one. The nine opening vectors were fixed from the archived known readings before the grid result was calculated. The same page-level rune selection includes headings and ignores layout marks. Planted encryptions with a 17-value key, a wrapped nonzero phase and both signs recovered their exact 12-rune text.

The [frozen plan](experiments/records/grid-prefix-split-openings/plan.json) pins the grid, page texts and opening traces by SHA-256. Run `python experiments/records/grid-prefix-split-openings/run.py` to regenerate the [group results](experiments/records/grid-prefix-split-openings/results.json), then `python experiments/records/grid-prefix-split-openings/check.py` for independent stream reconstruction and a full comparison recount.

The proposal also suggests treating the leading digits as directional route instructions. **No five-state direction table, origin or readout is specified**, so that different idea was not simulated here. Nor does this opening test examine later offsets, interruptions, nonrepeating keys or language scores.
